discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led the realisation of IceCube, a cubic-kilometre neutrino telescope built into the deep Antarctic ice. The idea is simple: use natural ice as a detector for Cherenkov light from neutrino interactions. Making it work at the South Pole was a very hard technical achievement. In 2013 IceCube reported the first detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin, reaching PeV energies. This opened a new observational window on the universe. Later results confirmed and sharpened it: evidence associating a neutrino with the flaring blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017-2018), neutrino emission from the active galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and from the Galactic plane (2023). Neutrinos are not deflected by magnetic fields and pass through matter, so they reveal the sites where cosmic rays are accelerated. This is a clearly identified discovery made possible by an invention, and it founded neutrino astronomy at high energies.
